p: Here's a fun one to drop on your mates: the man who designed Liverpool Cathedral, Giles Gilbert Scott, also designed the classic red telephone box. He was only in his early twenties when he won the competition to design the cathedral, and he spent much of the rest of his life on it. He's buried just outside, near the west end of the building he gave his career to.

If you've got a head for heights, the tower is the big extra. Head up and you get sweeping views over the city, the Mersey and, on a clear day, way beyond. It's a separate experience from simply walking in, so check what's running when you arrive.

Back at ground level, keep an eye out for Tracey Emin's pink neon artwork "For You", which glows above the west end and surprises plenty of first-timers. It's a nice reminder that this place isn't just about old stone. Allow an hour or so for a proper wander inside, and a bit longer if you're doing the tower or stopping for a cuppa.

Don't leave without peering down into St James' Gardens below the cathedral. It's a sunken former cemetery cut into an old quarry, and it's a peaceful, slightly atmospheric spot. Among those buried there is William Huskisson, the MP famously killed at the opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830.

Then walk the length of Hope Street. It links the Anglican cathedral with the Metropolitan Cathedral at the other end, the striking modern one locals nickname Paddy's Wigwam. In between you'll find the Philharmonic Hall, bars and places to eat, making it one of the nicest strolls in the city.
